Iron Maiden BY JOE FORDHAM n Yukito Kishiro's 1990 manga, Gunnm - translated as 'Gun Dream,' or Battle Angel Alita - a scientist discovers a broken cyborg in a futuristic scrapyard. He revives the robot, whom he names after his pet cat, 'Alita,' and pieces together the mystery of her origins in a story that unfolds over more than 850 pages of comic book art, depicting a nightmarish vision of a cyber-enhanced, 26th-century Earth. The comic's graphic stylings and enigmatic title character seemed tailor-made for filmmaker James Cameron. "Guillermo del Toro brought the project to our attention," recalled Cameron's Lightstorm Entertainment partner and producer Jon Landau. "It had all of Jim's trademarks - strong female protagonist, romantic story between two principals, cross-generational father-daughter relationship, and action that was out of this world, revolving around a teenage girl searching for her identity. I know that spoke to Jim as a father of three daughtersi Lightstorm, at the time, was on the cusp of another science fiction epic, Avatar. Back in 2005 going into 2006, we were torn as to which movie to do. We decided to do a test on the visual effects of performance capture and 1 / 29 for that we needed to pick a two-person scene, CG on CG. As fate would have it, Jim

ALITA picked a scene from Avatar, where Neytiri first met Jake in the bioluminescent forest, and that became the project we set our minds to. We decided to do Avatar first, and we'd bounce back to Alita when Jim was happy with that script. Nearly a decade later, while developing Avatar sequels, Cameron passed the Alita baton to filmmaker Robert Rodriguez for a Lightstorm co-production with Rodriguez's Troublemaker Studios and 20th Century Fox, entitled Alita: Battle Angel. Co-written by Cameron and Laeta Kalogridis, the film dramatized the first three volumes of Alita's story, beginning with Doctor Dyson Ido (Christoph Waltz) reviving the 300-year-old battle angel (Rosa Salazar), whom - in a twist on the manga - he names after his deceased daughter. Alita's paternal ties with Ido and her friendship with a street urchin, Hugo (Keean Johnson), living in the shadow of the floating city of Zalem, lead her to rediscover her Panzer Kunst martial arts skills she uses to combat a ruthless cybernetic trader, Vector (Mahershala Ali), and his cyborg hunter-warriors in a climactic battle in Iron City's brutal 'motorball' sports arena. Central to the project was the task of creating Alita as a slender, manga-proportioned cyborg. The character's evolution began in Lightstorm tests, predating Avatar, when filmmaker Stephen Norrington worked with Rhythm & Hues, Centropolis, Industrial Light & Magic and Cantina Creative to transform actor Timothy Carhart - wearing an alien prosthetic — into a spindly extraterrestrial adapted from a novel by Patricia Anthony. "I was running the visual effects facility for Rhythm & Hues' film division on a test for Brother Termite," recalled visual effects supervisor Richard Hollander. "We built a four-camera 2 / 29 helmet-mounted facial capture system to record the actor's face. We knew this technology

was coming around, either for Avatar or Battle Angel, but it seemed far off in the future." beyond. When Alita resurfaced under Rodriguez's aegis, Landau returned to Wellington, New Zealand. "Jon, Richard Hollander and Robert Rodriguez came out to visit us," recalled Weta Digital senior visual effects supervisor Joe Letteri. They showed us artwork and the script. Their focus was on Alita's performance, discovering who she was through her relationships with other characters. The designs, dating back to when Jim was developing the movie, were all based on the manga. One of the key decisions they made early on was in casting Rosa Salazar. Jon showed us a test they had shot with Rosa, and she was brilliant in nailing the feistiness and charm of the character. They were lucky to pick her almost right off the bat. We always like to bring as much as we can of a performer into a digital character. We spent a lot of time fusing Rosa's attributes with iconic aspects of the design - Alita's large eyes, her small mouth, her heart-shaped face, small chin, and her big head of hair. Those traits were all stylized in the comics, and we had to interpret those to turn Rosa into a three-dimensional character that felt real in every regard. Design concepts, initiated in 2005 with artists including James Clyne and Mark Goerner, informed production designer Steve Joyner and co-production designer Caylah Eddleblute at Troublemaker in Austin, Texas. Simultaneously, in California, Lightstorm designers Ben Procter and Dylan Cole led further concepts - with artists including Steve ALITA eta Digital ultimately ushered in a new era of performance-based animation for Avatar, building on its work with Gollum in The Lord of the Rings, and went on to hone capture processes on Planet of the Apes films and 3 / 29

Messing, Jonathan Berube and Fausto De Martini - to explore characters and world ALITA building.iWe wanted to come up with a visual language that honored the themes of the manga but felt real and grounded," said Dylan Cole, who focused on environments. "The most exciting aspect for me was how light and colorful Robert wanted the world to be. It wasn't the typical dark dystopian sci-fi we've seen so many times since Blade Runner. Iron City embraced a Latin American influence." The filmmakers extrapolated manga concepts of Zalem as a broken artery to an orbital space station. iWe decided the city was on the equator, possibly near Panama, given it required centrifugal force to connect it to the space station. We looked at a ton of references, like Havana, and threw science fiction elements on top. To the people of Iron City, Zalem represented a floating jewel in the sky. It had to feel aspirational and impressive but, for much of the story, characters lived in its shadow so it also had to feel somewhat sinister." Supply tubes connected the five-mile-wide airborne dish to robotic factories and a hydro-wall security perimeter around an industrialized favela.iIron City was old and rundown, with layers of textures and culture. And in the center, we had the scrapyard, where Zalem's trash had fallen, which is where Ido looks for parts and finds Alitai Lightstorm conceptual designer Ben Procter oversaw designs for Iron City's cyberaugmented citizens, incorporating James Cameron's concepts defining varying degrees of cyborg enhancements - from limb replacements to synthetic beings created to provide life-support for their functioning human brains. There were no androids, so to speak," explained Ben Procter. "Every cyborg had a human personality and probably 4 / 29 friends and family. There were limited exceptions to this rule in the factories. 'Hunter-

warriors' seek out anyone with a bounty on their head and receive rewards from 'DeckALITA men' - little robotic entities in the factory. Factory enforcer bots - 'Centurions' - also show a certain level of intelligence, but they're far from human. It's ultimately a human story, not a robot story. That vision was common to Jim's original ideas and the way the story manifested in Robert's script." Cyborg designs incorporated various degrees of augmentation, and KNB EFX Group explored possibilities for introducing makeup effects and practical robot pieces. "We did preliminary design work for an entire world of characters, background crowd and robotsi recalled KNB makeup effects supervisor Carey Jones, project leader for KNB co-founder Greg Nicotero. "We had a meeting at our L.A. studio, firing off ideas, and they encouraged us to come up with ways to incorporate practical makeups with Weta Digital's effects. Greg and I discussed using 'delineators' to establish where makeups would end and CGI would take over. We next had a presentation of designs and makeup tests at Troublemaker. That was helpful because the concepts in the script were so ornate, we weren't sure how much would be shot with makeup effects, motion capture, cardboard cutouts, or big foam gray suits. KNB key makeup artists Dave Snyder and Sabrina Wilson developed human/ robot blends for more than a dozen cyborg makeups.iFor all the main robotic characters and a lot of background characters, we took lifecasts. We sculpted onto those and created silicone prosthetics we blended to actors. If they wanted to give a guy a robotic arm, we made what we called a 'hard delineator' - if it was a shoulder piece, we built a rigid robotic shoulder prosthetic, which gave Weta an edge to define where to 5 / 29 remove gray parts and add digital piecesi

Robert got a great performance out of Rosa," stated Richard Hollander. "We knew we wanted to follow Rosa's lead. Weta Digital developed a toolset with head-cams, performance capture of her body and her head, plus reference cameras. That footage helped Weta to figure out performance, and film editor Stephen Rivkin used it to cut the film together. 'The partnership evolved, so while Joe, Eric and Mike worked on details, Richie served as an outside eye focusing on performance and facial animation. What I learned from Richie is it's never simply about a 'facial performance' — when a character's face is doing something, the body's attitude is affected and there are many facets to that. Richie has a great understanding of what goes into a performance and, having worked with Jim for years, he has developed an instinctive sense of camera. When we got to designing scenes that were 100 percent virtual, Richie played a big role in shot designi The translation of human performance to manga proportions involved restructuring physiognomy. "In our work with Jim on the Avatar films," said Richie Baneham, "we became obsessed with the behavior of the corner of the mouth, and the thickness of the ALITA 'o develop Alita's animated character, Hollander and Lightstorm visual effects creative supervisor Richie Baneham worked with a Weta Digital trifecta - Joe Letteri, visual effects supervisor Eric Saindon and animation supervisor Michael 6 / 29

mass of the inner cheek and inner mouth. That area is a soft tissue explosion of the priALITA mary muscles that come together as a huge intersection of articulation. Previously, we'd tended to think of that area a little more simplistically. The breakthrough came in recognizing the modiolus as a primary intersection of all of the musculature for the corner of the mouth. By breaking out animation controls to the inner and outer orbicularis muscles around her mouth, that gave the modiolus a sense of engagement and an attitude." At Weta Digital, Mike Cozens worked with Weta's facial model team to develop Alita's rigging, interpolated through a digital representation of the performer built from a topographical representation of Salazar's facial displacement. #It was a confidence check that our muscle rig was directly representing displacements on Rosa's face, Baneham explained. That allowed us to know our interpretation from Rosa to the muscle-driven actor puppet was giving us a credible representation of her performance. We could then interpret from the actor to the character.i The investment in facial muscle detail revealed hitherto unseen depth in animation. "We started to read subtleties almost down to inferred states of emotion. Those are the hardest details to read in CG. From the time we're babies, we're trained to recognize the emotional state of another person. Without thinking, we instantly assess whether a person looks upset or happy. When we started to read emotional states in relatively 'blank' expressions is when we started to feel synapses firing in the brain, triggering facial muscles and creating a real emotional state." Emotional interpretation was weighed with stylization. The manga look was there from the beginning," observed Ben Procter. "That was always a lynchpin for the movie Jim 7 / 29 and Robert wanted to make - the hair, the big eyes, that's Alita. If you don't have those

elements, it's not her. It was non-negotiable. "All of us were in agreement," added Richard Hollander. "Our biggest issue was Alita's face, the proportions of her head and how her hair was going to work. Our main concern was getting her to work in such a way that viewers were not stuck in the 'uncanny valley.' We wanted them to focus on the story. Alita's eyes were bigger and wider than a normal human's, and her head was shaped to accommodate that. Rosa's performance was our target, but we also wanted to create a feeling of being close to human, but not human. the shape of Rosa's eyes and mouth. It was similar to Avatar, where we translated the shape of Zoe Saldana's mouth into Neytiri, which allowed us to get the performance as close to the actress as possible. With Alita, Rosa's eyes, her eyebrows and eyelashes, and her mouth helped to bring Rosa's performance into Alita, and grounded her CG character in a reality I'm not sure we've seen before." #The safest way of retaining Rosa's performance was to make Alita look like the actress," added Joe Letteri. "We used that as background study for our actor puppet, to make sure we understood the performance capture. But we constantly had to look at how far we could push her into the character. There was no magic bullet for that. It took a lot of thought, and a lot of discussion. For our first few hundred shots, we were discovering the character." ALITA Performance capture ran the gamut of Weta procedures - witness cameras, computer vision, performance capture cameras and active markers for simulcam.iWe knew Rosa was going to play Alita in all the shots on set,i said Weta Digital performance capture supervisor Dejan Momcilovic.iWe had to provide a really good representation of her performance, which meant she was going to wear a facial helmet and markers we would capture. We used active LED body markers because a lot of scenes were on location, outdoors in the sunlight, unsuited to reflective markers. We worked with the costume designer to build a custom active marker suit for Rosa in dark gray fabric, pants and a jacket. There were no wires trailing out, and the suits were very flexible. We sewed channels through the suit to power eight strands of infrared LEDS, with zippers where all our gear could go. That enabled us to make sure all the markers were in the right place, and we could easily replace batteries and marker-drivers, which controlled LEDs on the suit and synchronized remotely to the Alexa cameras." The ubiquity of capture systems allowed Rodriguez to work with Salazar on set as Alita, in correct lighting, while the visual effects team observed size differences and interactions relative to the digital character's cyborg anatomy. We had two doubles who wore Alita's wardrobe," explained Richard Hollander. "We'd walk them through shot, for lighting and cloth behavior reference, and then we shot clean plates. That reference was important. Robert shot a lot of handheld and booming camera moves, native stereo with two cameras, which was something Jim and Robert believe in adamantly. Performance capture systems synchronized with stereographic ARRI Alexa cameras cinematographer 9 / 29 Bill Pope implemented with Cameron | Pace Fusion 3D technology. iWhen action was too

ALITA fast and furious, we sometimes shot with a single camera and Alexa Minis. Rosa's headmounted cameras were pointing at her face, and if ever they impeded her actions, we'd pull those off and shoot takes without. The rules were: we needed footage the editors could use, and we also needed technical information off her face - if those two things collided, we had to give up one." Weta Digital's motion capture team gathered data using its proprietary tracking and capture system, Whobble. They then exported data out of Autodesk MotionBuilder - using Weta's Atlas scene management system and real-time renderer, Gazebo - to solve Rosa Salazar's performance onto her human actor puppet. The methodology allowed Rodriguez to preview Alita, tracking the CG character to Salazar's performance during shooting. Alita facial capture took into account the requirements of shooting in native stereo. "This was the first show we shot with stereo pairs of facial cameras," noted Dejan Momcilovic. "We considered using a single-camera head-cam rig, but Jon Landau helped us convince Jim that a dual-camera stereo rig would be better; and it did make a difference. It was a step up in acquiring facial performance." Weta Digital's on-set data acquisition team worked in two units, playing leap-frog with production. "Alita worked almost every single day, so we had crews pre-rigging the next location and de-rigging the previous. The Iron City backlot set was so big, it took a couple of weeks to pre-rig all those buildings. The set was about 20 feet in height. We fitted our cameras on Speedrail pipe fittings and rigged that entire city with approximately 500 cameras." Weta Digital expanded a backlot set of Iron City's scrapyard, constructing a chaos 10 / 29 of technological detritus. "We built a rough layout for piles of debris based on the com-

position of each scene," related Eric Saindon. "We then used effects simulations to drop debris into the layout, allowing elements to fall and naturally build the volumesi Modelmakers detailed Zalem with architecture rising from its giant dish. We laid out a city five miles in diameter and built geometry based on building heights to create a layout of city streets to a proper grid and scale. In most real cities, a five-mile span progressively leads to smaller buildings, but we placed bigger buildings along the outside of the rim, so they'd be visible from Iron City. for digital replacement.iWe made several iterations of Alita parts including her partial body in the trash heap," said Carey Jones. "We also made a full-sized dummy Christoph could carry, and other insert pieces. We 3D-printed the body, head to toe, based on a Weta model, and then molded it, cast hard parts, and jointed those so it moved like a real body. We had different heads, including one where the neck was floppy, others where she was damaged and we could remove an arm or leg. Whenever characters touched parts of her body, Robert wanted something tangible there, so Weta could then use those interactions to replace our pieces with the digital Alita." Other featured cyborgs included the muscular and handsome hunter-warrior Zapan (Ed Skrein), who represents the luxury end of self-modification. selves," commented Ben Procter. "An impoverished factory worker has a giant yellow maALITA chine arm because it's required for his work. It's not a torture. He's happy to have that, and it's a point of pride he can provide for his family with this thing, but it's not an aesthetic choice. On the other end of the spectrum, we had people of greater wealth who have pimped their rides. Zapan has modified himself and he's quite taken with his own appearance. His armor style was metallic and muscular. We came up with a design for him that looked intimidating but had visual coherence, so his machine parts did not interpenetrate, and allowed him flexibility to get into poses." Zapan's human face was scalloped from a mechanical skull KNB outlined with delineators at a quarter-inch depth. Weta Digital grafted mechanisms behind the performer's cheekbones. "The cut-off was along the side of the face," Richard Hollander stated. "There was a lot of discussion as to how far we should go with less face and more mechanics. But Weta explained that unless the edge of the face was sharply connected, it would move all over the place. KNB's prosthetic delineators stiffened that edge and minimized its motion. We never blended mechanics into skin in a smooth line. To inform cybernetic proportions, KNB fabricated a gray body suit Ed Skrein wore on set. Weta Digital then extrapolated performance. "Zapan worked out well in the way his head connected to his machine body," noted Eric Saindon. "KNB placed their delineator far enough back so we weren't getting a lot of muscle pulls in that area. Where we attached his cybernetic body, we followed Ed's sternocleidomastoid muscles to pistons at his clavicle. Ed was a big guy, and we strove to keep his muscle tone through his cyber 12 / 29 parts so his human head fitted to his cyber body."

ALITA ackground cyborgs featured mixtures of practical and digital appendages. KNB B storm concepts, and output 3D-printed parts. KNB mold department supervisor Steven Frakes oversaw lifecasting and molding of urethane pieces, and prosthetic manufacturing department supervisor Derek Krout oversaw silicone prosthetics. We do a lot of 3D printing now at KNB," noted Carey Jones. "But when it comes to prosthetics, I'm always a fan of silicone lifecasting. 3D printing from a digital scan of a performer is never precise enough for our needs. When we're blending prosthetics to an actor's skin, we need pore detail you get from a silicone casting, especially if an appliance fits around the eyes. For every character we glued prosthetics to, we took lifecasts." Jones, Dave Snyder and Sabrina Wilson led prosthetic applications, alongside KNB fabrication department supervisors Beth Hathaway and Clare Mulroy who oversaw robotic parts, adding limb, chest and neck pieces for up to 60 crowd artists. Weta Digital enhanced featured cyborgs with performance captured animation. For Vector's lead hunter-warrior, Grewishka (Jackie Earle Haley), who menaces Alita in three mechanical incarnations, Lightstorm developed concept paintings and models in Chaos Group V-Ray 3D. "I roughed out paintings of Grewishka Mark One," said Ben Procter. Fausto De Martini then did a wonderful job taking Grew through his Mark Two and Mark Three stages, developing proportions and turning those into 3D models. Even before they cast Jackie Earle Haley, Fausto's keyframe concept art for Grew really captured the vibe of the patina on his metals, dripping with wateri 13 / 29 In early scenes, Grewishka appears as a looming figure in a robe. KNB created a full-

ALITA sized body suit stunt performer Keil Zepernick wore on stilts. When Grewishka is revealed at his full nine-foot height, Jackie Earle Haley and Zepernick performed simulcam depictions in virtual environments. "Jackie could see himself as Grewishka," said Dejan Momcilovic.iGrew had huge hands with clothing and chains that could easily intersect with his own body so it was important to give Jackie an idea of how his poses looked on the character. On set, as well as in the motion capture volume, Jackie delivered his dialogue on boxes, to place him at the correct height for eyelines. We then overlaid him with Grewishka, to inform camera framing, and generated playback live to picture, which allowed Robert to make adjustmentsi Weta Digital adapted Haley's performance to Grewishka's behemoth height and girth. We then built a completely digital face and giant body, following Grew through several incarnations as one of Alita's main opponents. At one point, there is an important back and forth with Grew, where Alita begins to get an inkling of who she is. It's an important scene for both characters and the key for us was to be true to Jackie's performance, while adding physicality to his giant character. We used Jackie's performance whole cloth. To sell Grew's physicality we slowed down the returns of his arm swings and added layers of physics. ALITA Hollander. iIdo attaches that to the body he had built for his daughter, who had been crippled at birth but died before he could apply it to her; and so, that body deepened his connection to Alita in the storyline. The first time we see her walk is in that body, and it set up all our rules. Ido gives her civilian clothes, and we discussed the idea of having Rosa wear clothes so we could attach Alita's head and hands through those. But Joe and Eric confirmed they preferred to create Alita entirely as a computer-generated image. A lot of talented people were involved in the design of that particular body - we called her 'cybergirl' - and it turned out to be a wonderful image. Lightstorm adapted Alita's design from manga illustrations, inferring a personalized creation that was a labor of love carved by a father for his daughter. 'It had to have a delicacy and exotic craftsmanship that was present in Kishiro's art, noted Ben Procter. "Robert urged us to use an alabaster finish, rather than porcelain. He didn't want a glossy china-doll vibe. Designer Vitaly Bolgarov created studies in ZBrush and Softimage XSI, rendered in KeyShot.iVitaly started with her hand, worked his way up the arm and collaged an amazing design, working with the translucent quality of alabasteri Weta Digital created Alita's cybergirl body as a high-resolution model revealing depth through the alabaster so internal mechanisms occluded light that permeated the alabaster. "We used blocker shapes to reveal shapes within her body," related Eric Saindon. "They shadowed the alabaster and created nice subsurface depth, like light through a wax candle." Weta layered details as Alita tests her body and bites into an orange. "We used the inside of Rosa's mouth in her chewing of the orange. We modeled her mouth- and lip15 / 29 shapes so closely, in that instance we rotoscoped Rosa's performance from the reference

plate and composited Rosa's chewing into Alita's mouth. • Because the outer shell was semi-transparent, the complex clockwork internals all had to be rigged to work together without intersecting. In some action scenes, she had to do the splits and very dynamic poses, so we built our CG puppet to describe those lines of action." Alita's cyborg anatomy emulated biological cues. "Breathing is something you might take for granted - but does a cyborg breathe? These were James Cameron questions we had to address. The choice was made that, yes, Alita does breathe because, in Rosa's performance, her breath was a big part of her emotional state, especially when Rosa exerted and then stopped to deliver a line. Without those breaths, we missed a level of complexity that helped to sell an emotional state and helped the viewer believe in the character." Salazar's emotions emerged through complex facial processes. We started with our actor puppet of Rosa," said Cozens. "We worked through performances with the human version of her as a one-to-one match with Rosa. That verified nuances of her facial performance and subtle muscle behavior. We used witness camera and face-camera data to verify that performance, and then transferred it to Alita. We spent a long time refining her eye size and facial proportions - and that went on in tandem with animation. While the design moved around, we had our Rosa-actor puppet to work on. It enabled us to get ALITA reature technical director Carlos Lin rigged Alita's interior mechanisms to respond to Salazar's performance. We spent a lot of time working with the creatures and models team to resolve Alita's complexity, said Mike Cozens. 16 / 29

ALITA her performance working on her human puppet, while her Alita design took shape. This was useful because it took a while to nail down Alita's final look; and it was also helpful for Robert because there's only so much you can do to design a character in concepts. It's not until you see a character rendered and lit in a shot that you can make a final call on design." Weta Digital created 176 versions of its Alita facial puppet over 18 months of postproduction. Tissue simulations referenced psychologist Paul Ekman's Facial Action Coding System of musculofacial expression, tempered with the requirements of more than 1,000 dialogue shots. "A lot of FACS shapes tend to be extreme," noted Cozens. "Happy,' 'mad' or 'sad,' all use extreme shapes. During dialogue, however, facial action is influenced by a much subtler range of motion. We ended up creating around 2,500 face-shape combinations for Alita - three times more than we'd created for Neytiri on Avatar. Weta Digital applied biological detail to the cyborg's eyes in Side Effects Houdini.iWe built Alita's eye using fibers for her iris and broke those fibers to emulate the way a real eye is built," said Eric Saindon. "The model for Alita's eye contained more geometry than all of Gollum in Lord of the Ringsi Alita's hair, which resembled a lion's mane in manga illustrations, required reinterpretation in Weta's hair simulation tool - Wig. Her manga hair would have been a big stiff mop if we'd matched the comics," remarked Joe Letteri. "We did styling tests to figure out how real hair would behave, and we went through many grooms. The art department tried some early tests with Rosa, with her hair relatively un-styled. Robert responded 17 / 29 well to that, so we created a style that was uniquely Alita, but with more realism.

ALITA The groom aligned with manga author Yukito Kishiro's perspective on Alita's evolution. "We noticed Alita's hair was much bigger in the first Alita book," said Eric Saindon. In subsequent years, the same bearded fellow could be glimpsed orchestrating previsualizations as part of Weta Digital's Oscar-winning visual effects team on King Kong. Check the home video features for the Hobbit films, and there he is again, Peter Jackson's taller Zelig, directing pick-up photography at Stone Street Studios while Jackson bore the weight of a second trilogy on his shoulders. The accomplice, Christian Rivers, a native of Whanganui in New Zealand's north island, has worn many hats for Jackson's WingNut Films. His latest and certainly grandest role is director of WingNut and Universal Pictures' Mortal Engines. The film, adapted from the first in a series of 'Predator Cities' novels by U.K. science fiction author Phillip Reeve, was a titanic undertaking. Set in a far-future post-apocalyptic world, characters traverse wastelands in behemoth wheeled cities that gobble up rival settlements based on the philosophy of 1 / 29 'Municipal Darwinism' espoused by Thaddeus Valentine (Hugo Weaving), lead historian

MORTAL ENGINES on the Traction City of London. Told from the point of view of Tom Natsworthy (Robert Sheehan), a lowly apprentice ejected from the city, the story traced a journey of discovery revolving around Tom's friendship with an outcast, Hester Shaw (Hera Hilmar), who is obsessed with killing Valentine, and Anna Fang (Jihae Kim), a freedom-fighting aviatrix, leader of the Anti-Traction League. The filmmakers' collaboration began when they met in the period between Jackson's 1989 monster puppet caper, Meet the Feebles, and WingNut's 1992 horror comedy Braindead - known in the U.S. as Dead Alive. "I was 18 and just out of high school," said Christian Rivers. I'd spent my childhood watching movies, drawing, playing Dungeons & Dragons, not really knowing what I wanted to do. Fangoria magazine had a story on Meet the Feebles. I'd seen Pete's first film, Bad Taste, but until then I hadn't put two and two together, and I thought I should get in touch with this guy. Rivers' sister's boyfriend, a model maker who had worked on director Vincent Ward's fantasy adventure The Navigator, provided a link to Jackson's brain trust at Weta Workshop. He said, 'If you want to get in touch with Peter Jackson, the best person to talk to would be Richard Taylor.' I called, and Richard, being his generous and enthusiastic self, invited me to send my artwork. I sent him a box of every drawing I'd ever drawn, not a professional portfolio. Cheekily, I called him the next day. Richard was busy, but he said: 'Oh, yes, sorry, mate. Peter loved your drawings. He really wants to meet you. When can you come down?'" Rivers' mother drove her son to Wellington, where Taylor redirected them to a well2 / 29 to-do waterfront suburb of Seatoun. "I looked at all the big houses going by," Rivers re-

called. I was thinking, 'Which of these is Pete's?' We got to the address and it was a little one-bedroom house with a garage. Inside, there was the car from Bad Taste and all the Meet the Feebles puppets and this smallish, bearded guy with curly black hair. I looked past him into a movie geek's hoarding dream - model kits up to the roof, Beatles posters everywhere, a sculpture of a goblin that he was doing, and a half-built World War I Fokker plane. I was expecting someone loud and brash, but Pete was quiet and polite, and he wanted to know what was I interested in and what kind of films I liked." ing ambitions. As the scope of Pete's films grew, I kept finding ways to keep creatively involved, and it's been a synergistic relationship. I've always been of use to Pete. On The Hobbit, Andy Serkis directed the lion's share of second unit, but when Andy left to work on Planet of the Apes, Pete asked me to shoot a splinter unit. Four sequels followed, each more bombastic than the last, each showcasing an ever-expanding ensemble of hyperkinetic Autobots and Decepticons waging war with extreme prejudice, and reducing many of Earth's most iconic cities to rubble in the process. In Transformers, no robot had more screen time than Bumblebee, a mute Autobot capable of disguising himself as a yellow Chevrolet Camaro. A deliberate transformation from the highly caffeinated cinematic style that came to be known as 'Bayhem,' screenwriter Christina Hodson's Bumblebee script drastically reduced the cast of characters and focused instead on the friendship between misfit teenager 1 / 27 Charlie Watson (Hailee Steinfeld) and Bumblebee, a lost robot warrior whose amnesia

has reduced him to a childlike state. "Bumblebee is really the story of the other," said BUMBLEBEE associate producer and visual effects producer Ron Ames. Travers (Emma Thompson) in her London home to persuade the recalcitrant author to go forward with Mary Poppins, his studio's film adaptation of Travers' beloved children's stories. Disney finally gains Travers' trust with his expressed understanding of what lies at the heart of those stories - namely, that Mary Poppins does not come to the Banks' home to rescue the children, but rather their father, George Banks. The father is again the central figure in need of saving in Mary Poppins Returns, starring Emily Blunt as the seemingly no-nonsense - but actually quite whimsical - nanny. Set in 1930s, Depression-era London, the story centers on the adult Michael Banks (Ben Whishaw), a recent widower with three young children, Anabel (Pixie Davies), John (Nathanael Salen) and Georgie (Joel Dawson). Having fallen on hard times, Michael is about to lose their home to the bank. All seems hopeless, until Mary Poppins re-enters the Bankses' lives, and with the help of sister Jane (Emily Mortimer) and a cheerful lamplighter - or 'leerie' - named Jack (Lin-Manuel Miranda), restores happiness to Number 1 / 29 17 Cherry Tree Lane.

MARY POPPINS Director Rob Marshall's attitude toward bringing the Mary Poppins sequel to the screen was one of fierce protectiveness regarding its 54-year-old progenitor, a film he recalls seeing when he was just four years old. "I distinctly remember being taken to see it," Marshall said, "which may sound crazy, given how young I was; but it made a huge impression on me. And, of course, I revisited it many times after that. Anytime there was a re-release of it, before there was VHS, I'd go see it. Mary Poppins is something I've lived with my whole life, and I know it deeply. So, when they asked me to do this, I thought, 'Well, if anyone is going to do this, I want to be the one' - because I loved the original film so much, and wanted to make sure we honored it, while at the same time creating something completely originali As it happened, Marshall - who had previously reimagined stage musicals such as Chicago and Into the Woods for the movies, to much acclaim - had long wanted to direct a musical created expressly for film.iMy favorite musical films are all from that golden era at MGM," Marshall stated, "like Singin' in the Rain, Meet Me in St. Louis and Bandwagon, all of which were created specifically for films. The challenge of taking a Broadway show to film is how to take it away from the proscenium, open it up and make it work as a movie. The best part of this process was that it was a movie, from the start; but at the same time, it didn't have the incubation time you get with a Broadway production, which has rehearsals and out-of-town previews. That's why this movie took three years to make from beginning to endi To develop the narrative of Mary Poppins Returns, Marshall and screenwriter David 2 / 29 Magee turned to Travers' original books, which hinted at the Depression era in which they

were written. "Travers writes about how the bank is broken," Marshall said, "and mentions that 17 Cherry Tree Lane, the Banks home, is the shabbiest house on the street. You get a sense of the struggle, in between the lines. So I thought we should set this film in the Depression era, 25 years after the events of the original. Michael and Jane have grown up. They are dealing with the harsh realities of life, and that has made them forget their childlike wonder and joy, which is a big theme of Travers' books. But then, Mary Poppins comes through the clouds as a ray of hope; and by healing this family, she brings hope to the story, and also to us, today. "We were in two different worlds on this film," commented Rob Marshall. "We were in the real, Depression-era world, which was in juxtaposition to the fantasy worlds that Mary Poppins launches the characters into. Our animation team really went through the fires in getting all these disparate greenscreen elements lined up in 3D space, moving together, with a camera that was flying by them and languidly floating over London - and have it look like the people were all in the same place at the same time, when in fact they were shot on different screens, with different cameras, and without motion controli In the end, Framestore built a comp-based animation rig into which they piped the tracked cameras from all of the different greenscreens into a single Nuke script. A compositor could then drive the different performers through 3D space," said McCulloch. Trying to do something like that in a regular animation pipeline proved to be nearly impossible. Running out of comp was the only way we could quickly turn around versions of pretty high quality, and get them in front of Rob so he could engage with them. The scene's aerial views of London offered some of the same challenges as the magical ocean sequence, in terms of finding an appropriate balance between realism and fantasy. "Much like the underwater stuff," said McCulloch, "the brief wasn't 'make it look totally real.' That was never what Rob was reaching for. But we couldn't think of it as a totally fairy tale environment, either. In the end, it was a matter of making it look real, and then taking some of that 'real' off. Our head of environments, Freddy Salazar, really came through with that, and he was tireless in creating those London environments, and 27 / 29 then adding a bit of a visual spin to make them look somewhat fantastic and idealized,

"We built an extraordinary number of trees and simulated all of them to make the environment feel alive and welcoming. We had a library of ten different species of trees, and the effects team ran custom simulations to make them move in a very particular manner. There was a tight connection between effects and the environments team so we could get that working quickly and get it in front of the directori n an era in which visual effects are more often than not in service to warring superheroes and aliens, Mary Poppins Returns was a breath of fresh springtime air for "the visual effects artists charged with creating its fantastical elements. "It has been such a pleasure to do this movie," commented Christian Kaestner. "We knew all the way through that we were working on something extraordinary and magical and special. It was a very different type of work for us. It wasn't blowing up buildings and explosions and that kind of thing. It was very creative, artistically-driven visual effects work. "The thing about Mary Poppins," added Matt Johnson, "is that it is a shared memory for many people. The music, the iconic images of London, the animated penguins dancing with Mary and Bert - all of that is part of our collective childhood. So when it came time to do this, it was a bit like Disney handing us the crown jewels. It felt extraordinarily special, right from the beginning, and then all the way through the shoot and postproduction. Every day, it seemed, something magical happened." 28 / 29
